content_units: 2017 Corolla Symptom Snapshot
Your pattern points most strongly to a   minor air/fuel or ignition issue developing gradually  , rather than a sudden major failure.

The combination of   occasional rough idle + slower acceleration + worse fuel economy   with   no warning light   is often caused by maintenance-related items or a sensor/airflow issue that has not yet triggered a fault code.
Most Likely Causes and Owner-Safe Checks
Cause   Why it fits your symptoms   Safe checks you can do   Usual repair cost level
Dirty engine air filter   Reduced airflow can hurt acceleration and fuel economy   Open airbox, inspect filter for dirt/leaves/dark clogging   Low-cost
Dirty throttle body   Common cause of rough idle and lazy throttle response   Look for carbon buildup at throttle opening; do not force plate open on electronic throttle   Low-cost

Aging spark plugs   At 118,000 km, plugs are a very plausible cause of rough idle and reduced efficiency   Review service history; if original plugs are still installed, they are due/overdue on many schedules   Low-cost to moderate

Weak ignition coil beginning to fail   Can cause intermittent rough running before a warning light appears   Listen/feel for slight shaking at idle; note if worse under load or damp weather   Moderate

MAF sensor contamination   Incorrect airflow reading can cause rich/lean running and poor mileage   Check intake tube for loose clamps/cracks; inspect sensor area only, avoid touching sensor wire   Low-cost

Tire pressure / dragging brakes   Can worsen fuel economy and make the car feel sluggish   Check all tire pressures cold; after a drive, carefully compare wheel heat for one abnormally hot wheel   Low-cost to moderate
Fuel injector deposits   Can cause rough idle, reduced power, and increased consumption   Notice if idle smooths slightly after a longer highway drive or with fresh top-tier fuel   Moderate
PCV / vacuum leak   Small leaks can create rough idle and fuel trim issues without immediate warning light   Inspect visible hoses for cracks, loose ends, oil residue, split rubber   Low-cost
Old or incorrect engine oil   Excess friction can slightly affect economy and response   Confirm oil level and condition; verify correct viscosity from invoice/manual   Low-cost

Early O2 / A/F sensor aging   Can reduce fuel economy before setting a code   Usually needs scan tool data; owner check is mainly noting sulfur smell, rich exhaust smell, poor mileage trend   Higher-cost

Sticky brake caliper or wheel bearing drag   Causes fuel economy drop and sluggishness   After short drive, compare wheel temperatures carefully; car pulling slightly can be a clue   Moderate to higher-cost
Low fuel pressure / weak pump   Can cause hesitation and weaker acceleration   Hard to verify safely without tools; note if issue worsens at low tank levels or high load   Higher-cost
Practical At-Home Inspection Plan
Do these in order, because they are safe and most likely to reveal something useful:
Option 1: Check tire pressure and wheel drag   Fastest way to explain a mileage drop   Aim for door-jamb spec, not tire sidewall
Tire guide
Option 2: Inspect the air filter   Very common and cheap fix if dirty   Replace if heavily darkened or debris-filled
Filter basics
Option 3: Review maintenance history for spark plugs   118,000 km puts plugs high on the list   If never changed, move this near the top
Toyota manuals
Option 4: Check intake hose and vacuum lines   Cracks/loose clamps can cause rough idle   Look for split rubber, disconnected small hoses
Hose inspection
Option 5: Check oil level and condition   Low or degraded oil can affect smoothness   Check on level ground with engine off after a few minutes
Oil care
Option 6: Note when symptoms are worst   Helps separate ignition, fuel, and drag issues   Idle only, cold start only, uphill load, A/C on, wet weather, low fuel level
Low-Cost vs Higher-Cost Repairs
Usually low-cost
-   Engine air filter replacement
-   Throttle body cleaning
-   MAF sensor cleaning   using proper MAF cleaner only
-   Spark plug replacement   if access is straightforward
-   PCV valve or small vacuum hose replacement
-   Tire pressure correction / wheel alignment check
-   Fuel system cleaner   as a mild first step, if no severe drivability issue
Usually moderate
-   Ignition coil replacement
-   Professional injector cleaning
-   Brake service for light dragging
-   Battery/charging check if idle quality changes with A/C or lights on
Usually higher-cost
-   A/F sensor or oxygen sensor replacement
-   Fuel pump or fuel pressure regulator work
-   Brake caliper replacement if seized
-   Wheel bearing replacement
-   Catalytic converter issue   if power loss becomes much worse later
Best Next Step for This Corolla
The most plausible order for your case is:
1.   Air filter / intake leak / tire pressure
2.   Spark plugs
3.   Dirty throttle body or MAF sensor
4.   Early ignition coil weakness
5.   Small vacuum leak or brake drag
6.   A/F sensor or fuel delivery issue

Because there is   no warning light  , this still sounds like a problem that may be caught early and fixed relatively cheaply. If the plugs are original, that is one of the strongest suspects at   118,000 km  .
